summary: Describes an anycasting service for IP, in which a packet goes to any one of a group of hosts that provide the same service. It mainly establishes what such a service should mean.

plainLanguage.summary: IP anycasting lets a sender address a group of servers that offer the same service without choosing one server by name. The network tries to deliver a packet to one server, but it does not guarantee that later packets reach the same one.

questions: how does anycast work with tcp
what are the security issues with anycast
subtitle: A proposed IP service that delivers a packet to one of several service hosts.

tldr.problem: An application may need any server offering a service, but choosing a server from a list requires the application to select one itself.
tldr.mechanism: An anycast address represents a group of servers. IP makes a stateless, best-effort attempt to deliver each datagram to at least one, and preferably one, server in the group.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1546 is an Informational description of an experimental service. It establishes semantics and does not propose a protocol.

facts.label: Delivery
facts.value: Best effort to at least one server

facts.label: TCP use
facts.value: Remote address of SYN without ACK

today: RFC 1546 is an Informational memo from November 1993, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes an experimental service and proposes no protocol.

sections.title: The Anycast Service
sections.content:
Internet Protocol (IP) anycasting is for a host, application or user that wants a server providing a service but does not care which server responds. The sender transmits a datagram to an anycast address, and the internetwork makes a best-effort attempt to deliver it to at least one server that accepts that address.

The RFC gives examples including a user reaching an Archie server, a DNS resolver sending a query to a well-known anycast address, and mirrored FTP servers sharing an address. The memo defines the intended service behavior, not an implementation protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender addresses the service, not a particular server. The network tries to deliver the datagram to a server that accepts that anycast address.

sections.title: What Delivery Does and Does Not Guarantee
sections.content:
IP anycasting is stateless best-effort delivery. One datagram may reach more than one server, and two datagrams sent to the same anycast address may reach different servers.

IP does not remember which server received earlier packets. An application or stateful transport that needs to continue with the same server must use an additional mechanism; the RFC suggests learning that server's unicast address during the first exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: The network does not promise to choose only one server or to choose the same server twice. Applications that need a continuing conversation must identify a server and use its unicast address.

sections.title: Anycast Addresses and Packet Delivery
sections.content:
The RFC considers using existing IP address space, reserving a separate class, or taking a portion of the existing space such as 256 Class C addresses. It favors a separate address class because it would be easier to recognize and could support well-known anycast addresses, while noting routing costs as a disadvantage.

On a shared network, a host could use ARP to find a local server or send to a link-level multicast address. On point-to-point links, a router forwards one copy toward the destination. Hosts that provide an anycast service must advertise that they support the address.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo considers several ways to distinguish anycast addresses and favors a separate address class. On a local shared network, a sender can use ARP or link-level multicast to reach a server.

sections.title: Transport Protocols and Multicast
sections.content:
UDP can treat anycast addresses like other IP addresses because UDP is stateless. TCP is stateful, so the RFC permits an anycast address only as the remote address of an initial SYN without ACK; after receiving the SYN-ACK, the initiating TCP uses the responding host's address.

Unlike multicast, anycast is a special use of unicast routing and does not require the sender to expand the IP TTL to search for a server. The RFC notes a trade-off: multicast can reach other servers when one fails, while anycast packets may continue to be routed to a failed server.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP can start with an anycast address, then switch to the address of the server that replied. Multicast sends to a group, while anycast routing tries to reach one server.

sections.title: Security Risks
sections.content:
The memo identifies two security concerns and does not propose solutions. A malicious host could claim to serve an anycast address and divert datagrams from legitimate servers.

A host could also answer a query with inaccurate information. The memo says there is no way in the described service to verify membership in an anycast address and detect that such a host is not a legitimate member.
sections.plainLanguage: A host could falsely claim to provide an anycast service or return inaccurate information. This memo does not define a way to verify that a responding host is a legitimate member.
